items.title: Neuroimaging study links heightened sensitivity to peer rejection with harsher parenting after childhood abuse
items.summary:
More severe childhood abuse is linked to harsher discipline of teenagers among mothers whose brains react more strongly to social rejection than to social approval, according to a study published in Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience .

Among mothers without this heightened brain reactivity to negative social feedback, abuse severity was not associated with harsher parenting. The findings suggest that how the adult brain processes interpersonal slights and acceptance may help identify which families face greater risk of carrying mistreatment across generations.

Why childhood abuse does not always lead to harsh parenting 
 Childhood maltreatment includes abuse, involving physical, emotional, or sexual acts that harm or threaten a child, and neglect, the failure to provide expected care and stimulation. Mistreated children are two to three times more likely to mistreat their own children as parents, often through harsh discipline such as yelling, verbal hostility, physical punishment, or punishing without explanation. Evidence from a 2019 meta-analysis of 142 studies indicates that abuse persists across generations more consistently than neglect.

Because abuse involves interpersonal threat, how people process social feedback, meaning signals of approval, criticism, or rejection, may shape intergenerational risk. Adults who survived childhood abuse tend to display a negativity bias, such as reading neutral faces as angry or viewing ambiguous child behavior as defiant. Consistent with this, a 2011 longitudinal study of 499 mothers and their infants found that…

items.title: Reanalysis of 1950s LSD experiments challenges the idea that psychedelics make art more creative
items.summary:
Professional artists who painted under the influence of LSD produced markedly more abstract works than they did before taking the drug, according to a new reanalysis of archived mid-century artworks published in Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts . At the same time, blind evaluations by art experts detected no meaningful boost in the paintings’ overall creativity or aesthetic appeal, and no reliable drop in technical skill. The findings indicate that while psychedelic experiences can shift an artist’s visual style toward abstraction, they do not necessarily make the finished work more creative.

Lysergic acid diethylamide, commonly known as LSD, is a potent hallucinogenic substance that alters visual perception, emotion, and thought primarily by stimulating specific serotonin receptors in the brain. Alongside renewed clinical interest in psychedelic substances over the past two decades, anecdotal accounts from technology workplaces and visual arts communities have popularized the claim that taking LSD in either tiny microdoses or full hallucinogenic amounts can unlock artistic breakthroughs. Yet subjective impressions during a drug experience can be misleading, making it difficult to tell whether a substance genuinely improves creative work or merely makes ideas feel deeper in the moment.

In psychological science, creativity is typically defined as the ability to produce something that is both original and fitting or effective for its context. Reaching that balance requires two complementary modes of thinking: divergent thinking, which involves loosening…
items.t: Reanalysis of 1950s LSD experiments challenges the idea that psychedelics make art more creative

items.title: Common classroom accommodations for ADHD fail to improve student behavior or schoolwork in clinical trial
items.summary:
A clinical trial published in JAMA Pediatrics provides evidence that four widely used classroom accommodations for children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) do not improve student behavior or academic performance. In contrast, structured behavioral classroom supports and a moderate dose of stimulant medication both substantially reduced classroom rule-breaking, while medication also increased assignment completion and quiz scores.

The findings suggest that schools seeking to help students with ADHD succeed may achieve better results from active behavioral strategies than from standard classroom accommodations.

Why classroom accommodations for ADHD needed a test 
 ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by ongoing difficulties sustaining attention, curbing impulsive actions, and regulating physical restlessness. In elementary school classrooms, those traits frequently surface as trouble staying seated, following classroom rules, completing independent worksheets, and keeping up with group lessons.

In the United States, roughly half of students diagnosed with ADHD receive formal educational services through individualized education programs under federal special education law or Section 504 plans under disability civil rights law. These plans routinely center on academic accommodations, which are adjustments to classroom surroundings, work schedules, or testing conditions meant to help students complete the same assignments as their classmates. Common examples include extra time on assignments and quizzes, frequent short breaks,…
items.t: Common classroom accommodations for ADHD fail to improve student behavior or schoolwork in clinical trial

items.title: Six Factors That Support Mental Health for Black Youth
items.summary:
On a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an important public health concern. They were having fun even as they took on a heavy task: helping researchers design programs to reduce the skyrocketing suicide rate among Black youth. 

In the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades. For those between 10 and 17 years of age, the suicide rate rose 144% from 2007 to 2020 . What’s more, Black boys die by suicide more than twice as frequently as Black girls, although the suicide rate for Black girls increased by 182% between 2001 and 2017 .

As the teenagers brainstormed, Jasmin Brooks Stephens , a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby. The moment was a highlight in research she was conducting with the Homeless Children’s Network on improving mental health outcomes for Black youth. Brooks Stephens believed that teens themselves have meaningful ideas to share, and she had worked for eight weeks with these particular teenagers, who were part of the network’s Jabali Youth Advocacy organization, culminating in their trip to campus.

“One of the most exciting things was seeing them all jump up and say, ‘Wait, we can make a program for making us feel better? We have the power to do that?’” Brooks Stephens recalled. “Seeing them find and discover that sense of agency in themselves—that was invaluable to me.” It also was one of the few times any of the teens had visited a college campus, she said, an added bonus. In future work, Brooks Stephens plans to…
items.t: Six Factors That Support Mental Health for Black Youth

items.title: Why stopping SSRIs can cause anxiety: A rebound in serotonin neuron activity may play a role
items.summary:
A study of male mice found that stopping treatment with the SSRI antidepressant paroxetine was associated with increased activity in two brain areas involved in anxiety, the dorsal raphe nucleus and the ventral hippocampus. These changes appeared two days after treatment ended, when the mice also showed elevated anxiety-like behavior. Five days after discontinuation, the anxiety-like behavior had subsided, but activation of serotonin-producing neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus persisted. The paper was published in Neuropharmacology .

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs, are a widely used class of antidepressant medications. They are commonly prescribed to treat depression and some anxiety disorders. SSRIs work by blocking the reabsorption of serotonin, a neurotransmitter involved in regulating mood and other psychological processes, thereby increasing its availability in the brain.

However, abruptly stopping SSRI treatment can cause withdrawal-like symptoms, including increased anxiety, sleep disturbances, and unusual sensory experiences. These symptoms typically appear within a few days of discontinuation and can persist for several weeks or even longer. Animal studies have shown that stopping SSRI treatment can also produce behavioral changes resembling anxiety, including increased vigilance and avoidance of potentially threatening environments.

Previous research by the same team found that anxiety-like behavior in mice appeared two days after paroxetine was discontinued but had disappeared by five days, although disturbances in sleep and reduced…
items.t: Why stopping SSRIs can cause anxiety: A rebound in serotonin neuron activity may play a role

items.title: Focused ultrasound aimed deep into the brain may ease delusions, pilot study suggests
items.summary:
A small pilot trial suggests that aiming gentle, noninvasive sound waves deep into the brain may temporarily ease delusions in adults living with chronic psychosis. In a randomized comparison against a fake stimulation session, 10 outpatients who received 10 minutes of low-intensity focused ultrasound directed at a deep brain hub showed a moderate drop in delusion severity without experiencing serious side effects. The preliminary findings were published in npj Acoustics .

Schizophrenia and related conditions such as schizoaffective disorder are chronic psychiatric illnesses that alter how a person perceives reality, thinks, and relates to the world around them. Two hallmark psychotic symptoms are hallucinations, such as hearing voices when no one is speaking, and delusions, which are fixed beliefs that persist even when contradicted by everyday evidence. Standard antipsychotic medications quiet these symptoms for many patients, yet a substantial number continue to experience distressing delusions despite ongoing drug treatment.

Brain-imaging studies link psychosis to abnormal signaling along a deep loop of neural pathways connecting the cerebral cortex, the brain’s outer layer, with central relay structures called the striatum, the globus pallidus, and the thalamus. Tucked near the middle of the brain beneath the cortex sits the globus pallidus interna, a paired cluster of nerve cells within the basal ganglia that serves as a primary output gate sending dopamine-influenced signals to the thalamus. Beyond helping coordinate physical movement, this pathway helps filter…
items.t: Focused ultrasound aimed deep into the brain may ease delusions, pilot study suggests

items.title: Mindfulness therapy alters brain waves in major depressive disorder
items.summary:
Combining mindfulness training with standard antidepressant medication reduces depression symptoms more effectively than medication alone while simultaneously altering electrical activity in the brain. The new research, published in the journal Mindfulness , reveals that adding cognitive therapy centered on awareness to a patient’s routine care leads to distinct shifts in brain waves associated with emotional regulation.

Major depressive disorder involves persistent low mood, loss of interest in daily activities, and physical or cognitive changes that can severely disrupt a person’s life. The condition is associated with altered functional connections in the brain, particularly in networks responsible for processing emotions and self-referential thoughts. Standard treatments often include medications like antidepressants, but a large portion of patients do not experience full relief from these drugs alone. To improve outcomes, clinicians sometimes supplement medication with additional psychological therapies.

One such intervention is mindfulness-based cognitive therapy. This group-based psychosocial treatment combines meditation practices, such as deep breathing and guided body scans, with cognitive behavioral strategies designed to break patterns of negative thinking. The therapy aims to help patients observe their thoughts without judgment, which may prevent the spiral of rumination that often leads to a relapse of depressive symptoms.

Lead researcher Seyed Ruhollah Hosseini of Ferdowsi University of Mashhad in Iran and colleagues conducted the study to explore how…
items.t: Mindfulness therapy alters brain waves in major depressive disorder

items.title: Daily peanut consumption may improve brain insulin responsiveness in older adults
items.summary:
Eating about two handfuls of unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts every day for four months may alter how memory-related areas of the aging brain respond to the hormone insulin, according to a clinical trial published in Food & Function .

In a randomized study of healthy older adults, daily peanut intake shifted blood-flow responses to an insulin nasal spray within a right-hemisphere brain cluster that includes part of the hippocampus, even as liver fat, blood sugar, and cholesterol levels remained largely unchanged. The findings point to a potential biological pathway that could help explain why regular peanut consumption has been linked to better memory in older age.

How insulin acts in the aging brain 
 Insulin is a hormone produced by the pancreas that is best known for helping cells throughout the body absorb sugar from the bloodstream. Although the brain takes up most of its glucose without insulin’s help, dense concentrations of insulin receptors sit on brain cells in regions such as the prefrontal cortex, the hypothalamus, and the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the temporal lobe that is essential for forming and recalling memories.

“The hormone insulin plays an important role in the brain, where it supports memory and other cognitive processes,” principal investigator and senior author Peter J. Joris , an associate professor in the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences at the Institute of Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism at Maastricht University, told PsyPost.

Brain insulin responsiveness refers to the ability of specific…
items.t: Daily peanut consumption may improve brain insulin responsiveness in older adults

items.title: GLP-1 drugs linked to reduced alcohol use and healthier eating in real-world study
items.summary:
Adults taking popular diabetes and weight-loss medications tended to cut back on alcohol and stick more closely to healthy diets over nearly a year of routine medical care, according to a new study published in Addictive Behaviors . Patients also reported feeling calm and peaceful more often, although broad measures of overall mental health and long-term physical activity did not show meaningful changes. The findings add real-world clinical evidence to growing scientific interest in how metabolic drugs might relate to everyday habits beyond blood sugar and weight control.

Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, a class of medications that includes drugs such as semaglutide and dulaglutide, mimic a natural hormone released in the gut after eating. By binding to specialized proteins called receptors on cells in the pancreas, stomach, and brain, these drugs stimulate insulin release, slow digestion, and promote feelings of fullness. Doctors prescribe them widely to lower blood sugar in people with type 2 diabetes and to support weight loss in people with obesity.

Receptors for this hormone are not limited to regions that manage hunger and digestion. They also appear in the mesolimbic system, a network of deep brain structures that processes pleasure, motivation, and reward by releasing the chemical messenger dopamine. Animal experiments indicate that activating these receptors dampens dopamine surges triggered by addictive substances and reduces alcohol-seeking behavior.

Human studies have begun testing whether similar patterns emerge in medical patients. In…
items.t: GLP-1 drugs linked to reduced alcohol use and healthier eating in real-world study

items.title: Heavy cannabis use linked to mild psychotic symptoms and depressive thoughts
items.summary:
Frequent cannabis consumption is associated with a higher rate of mild hallucinations, unusual thoughts, and depressive symptoms compared to occasional use or abstinence. Starting cannabis at a younger age also correlates with an increase in these subclinical symptoms. The findings were published in the Journal of Psychiatric Research .

Psychotic-like experiences are phenomena that resemble the symptoms of psychotic disorders like schizophrenia but occur at a much lower intensity. They can include mild paranoia, hearing occasional whispers, or holding highly unusual beliefs. These experiences do not mean a person has a psychiatric disorder.

About seven to thirteen percent of the general population report having these mild perceptual experiences at some point. While often harmless, these subclinical symptoms can sometimes act as early warning signs for future mental health conditions.

In psychiatric terminology, symptoms fall into distinct categories. Positive symptoms refer to the addition of abnormal experiences, such as hallucinations or delusions. Negative symptoms refer to a loss of typical emotional responses, such as a lack of motivation, social withdrawal, or a flattened affect. Depressive symptoms involve persistent sadness and low energy.

University of Turin psychiatrist Valerio Ricci and his colleagues noticed a gap in the existing scientific literature regarding these symptoms. Past investigations often focused exclusively on healthy community volunteers or individuals already diagnosed with severe psychotic disorders.

The researchers wanted to study people…
items.t: Heavy cannabis use linked to mild psychotic symptoms and depressive thoughts

items.title: Does personality predict family size? A 15,000-person study across three countries weighs in
items.summary:
Adults who are more outgoing, cooperative, and emotionally stable tend to have slightly more biological children, according to a cross-cultural survey of more than 15,000 people across Canada, the United States, and Japan. Published in Culture and Evolution , the research also indicates that how personality relates to family size depends on national culture alongside major demographic factors such as marriage and age.

Psychologists commonly organize human personality using a framework known as the Big Five, which measures where individuals fall along five broad spectrums of thought, feeling, and behavior. Openness to experience reflects curiosity and receptivity to new ideas, conscientiousness captures organization and self-discipline, extraversion describes sociability and assertiveness, agreeableness involves warmth and cooperation, and neuroticism refers to a tendency toward anxiety, moodiness, and emotional distress. In evolutionary psychology, researchers examine how traits like these relate to reproductive success, defined concretely as the number of biological children a person has.

Personality shapes how people find romantic partners and maintain long-term relationships, which in turn can affect family size. Warmth and dependability tend to foster supportive partnerships, whereas high anxiety and emotional reactivity are linked to relationship strain and lower sexual satisfaction. In Western populations, a 2011 study of more than 15,700 American adults found that both men and women who scored higher in extraversion and openness and lower in neuroticism had more…
items.t: Does personality predict family size? A 15,000-person study across three countries weighs in

items.title: A 30-minute walk helps sustain brain activity during mental task switching, study finds
items.summary:
A small neuroimaging study found that a 30-minute moderate-intensity walk changed patterns of brain activity during a task requiring cognitive flexibility, and that some of these changes differed by age. After walking, activation in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex remained stable in older adults but declined in young adults, while activation in several parietal regions held steady after walking but declined after sitting in both age groups. Task performance, however, did not change. The paper was published in the Journal of Magnetic Resonance Imaging .

Aerobic exercise is physical activity, such as brisk walking, running, swimming, or cycling, that increases heart rate and breathing. It is called aerobic because, during such activities, muscle cells produce most of their energy through aerobic cellular respiration, a process that uses oxygen to extract energy from fats and carbohydrates. Studies indicate that a single session of aerobic exercise may temporarily improve cognitive performance. However, scientists do not yet fully understand how this happens.

One cognitive ability potentially affected by aerobic exercise that researchers have been particularly interested in is executive function. Executive function is a set of mental processes that allow people to plan, control their behavior, and pursue goals. An important component of executive function is cognitive flexibility, which is the ability to switch between tasks and adapt to changing circumstances. This ability relies on several interconnected brain regions, particularly those in the frontal and…
items.t: A 30-minute walk helps sustain brain activity during mental task switching, study finds

items.title: Scientists finally pin down what a mysterious Alzheimer’s gene does
items.summary:
Deleting an Alzheimer’s-linked gene called CASS4 in mice impairs the ability of brain immune cells to surround and compress toxic protein plaques, according to new research published in Journal of Experimental Medicine .

Without this gene, mice bred to develop Alzheimer’s-like pathology accumulated larger, looser plaques, suffered worse nerve-fiber damage, and struggled to adapt when a learned task changed. The findings indicate that CASS4 helps immune cells maintain the internal anchoring machinery needed to move toward brain damage and contain harmful deposits.

A cancer-linked gene inside the brain’s immune cells 
 Alzheimer’s disease is a progressive neurological condition that erodes memory and thinking, marked in the brain by clumps of amyloid-beta protein and tangled tau fibers. Genetic research increasingly points to microglia, the resident immune cells stationed inside the brain and spinal cord that sweep branching arms through tissue to watch for injury or disease. Human brain mapping, including an analysis of 3.4 million individual brain cells , suggests that after a gradual early loss of certain inhibitory neurons, Alzheimer’s shifts into a rapid phase of widespread inflammation, microglial changes, and accelerating plaque buildup.

Many inherited DNA variations tied to late-onset Alzheimer’s sit near genes active mainly in microglia. One prominent example is CASS4, first linked to Alzheimer’s risk in a 2013 genetic meta-analysis of more than 74,000 people . Microglia are virtually the only resident brain cells that switch this gene on, yet what CASS4 does in…
items.t: Scientists finally pin down what a mysterious Alzheimer’s gene does

items.title: How Becoming a Parent Can Change Your Memories of Your Own Parents
items.summary:
It was around Christmas time when Emily* noticed that something was wrong. She had just welcomed her second son in September and still felt emotionally raw from the experience. Part of Emily’s postpartum planning had revolved around having her mum look after her three-year-old while she took care of the new baby. But every time she visited her parents, something in her tensed up, her mind went foggy, and instead of feeling the safety and relaxation she had been craving, she felt on edge. 

Emily sought help from me in therapy just before Christmas when she realized that the prospect of spending the holidays with her parents was making it difficult for her to sleep and the few precious hours she had between feeds were taken up with anxious rumination. She couldn’t make any sense of it. It was like a switch had flipped and the previously supportive, albeit slightly emotionally disconnected, relationship she had had with her parents was in pieces.

I work a lot with mothers and birthing people in the perinatal phase, and the change they experience in their relationship with their parents is something that comes up very frequently. Sometimes this change is positive, where they become more understanding of parents who were trying their best at the time. Sometimes it’s disorienting, like Emily’s, and the relationship seems to worsen. Either way, it’s important to meet yourself with compassion and curiosity when unexpected feelings or memories resurface during this period of your life and try not to go through this transition on your own. 

Renegotiating our childhood memories…
items.t: How Becoming a Parent Can Change Your Memories of Your Own Parents

items.title: Childhood trauma and ADHD independently fuel risky driving habits, study suggests
items.summary:
Young adults who experience symptoms of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder or who have a history of childhood trauma report higher rates of unsafe driving behaviors. However, a new study reveals that while both factors independently increase the likelihood of dangerous driving, childhood adversity does not amplify the risks associated with the disorder. These findings were published in the journal Psychological Reports .

Motor vehicle crashes are a leading cause of death among young adults in the United States. Safety organizations estimate that tens of thousands of people die in traffic accidents every year. Drivers between the ages of 15 and 29 face a particularly high risk on the road. Identifying the underlying psychological factors that contribute to this heightened risk can help experts design targeted safety interventions and reduce traffic fatalities.

Psychology researchers frequently study attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, known as ADHD, as a major risk factor for negative driving outcomes. ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition defined by persistent patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Inattention involves difficulty sustaining focus or wandering off task. Hyperactivity and impulsivity involve excessive motor activity or making hasty actions without considering the consequences.

Young adults with ADHD often experience more driving citations, license suspensions, and car crashes than their peers. Yet, not all drivers with ADHD face the exact same level of risk. Many individuals with the condition do not experience crashes; one…
items.t: Childhood trauma and ADHD independently fuel risky driving habits, study suggests

items.title: New psychology study suggests your sexual turn-ons are far more fluid than assumed
items.summary:
What people find sexually arousing does not necessarily stay locked in place throughout adulthood. A new study published in Psychology & Sexuality indicates that adults generally view their sexual “turn-ons” as moderately changeable over time and across life experiences, with noticeable differences across age, race, gender, sexual orientation, education, and religion. Having shifting arousal triggers, however, showed no positive or negative connection with anxiety, depression, or sexual difficulties.

How shifting turn-ons differ from broader sexual fluidity 
 Sexual turn-ons are the specific qualities, situations, or sensations that spark sexual arousal, ranging from a partner’s physical features and personality traits to the emotional bond between partners. To describe changes in these triggers, researchers introduced the concept of “turn-on fluidity,” meaning the degree to which what sexually arouses someone shifts over time, through personal experiences, or across relationships. In a 2024 survey study by two of the same authors using data from the same broader research project, cisgender and gender-diverse adults reported an expansive mix of physical, personality, and relational turn-ons, raising the question of whether those preferences stay fixed or evolve.

Prior research on changing desires focused mostly on broad behavioral adaptability or on which genders someone finds attractive. In a 2000 theoretical review , the author argued that sexual desires and behaviors, especially among women, can be reshaped by culture and life circumstances, a capacity termed erotic…
items.t: New psychology study suggests your sexual turn-ons are far more fluid than assumed

items.title: Past experiences with classical music predict a taste for sophisticated genres
items.summary:
Children and teenagers who have spent time listening to classical music are more likely to appreciate complex musical styles like jazz and opera. A recently developed survey tool indicates that past emotional engagement with classical music is linked to a stronger preference for these genres. The research was published in the journal Psychology of Music .

Psychologists classify genres like classical, opera, jazz, and world music under the umbrella term of sophisticated music. The MUSIC model is a standard framework researchers use to categorize auditory tastes. In this model, sophisticated music is characterized by its perceived complexity and by being predominantly instrumental. Listeners generally perceive these genres as intelligent and inspiring.

Most children and teenagers gravitate toward pop, rock, or contemporary music in their daily lives. They rarely select sophisticated music to regulate their moods or socialize with friends. Music education programs frequently attempt to increase appreciation for classical music among younger generations. 

Past studies have shown that young children are generally open to many types of music. This openness to different styles narrows dramatically during adolescence. During the teenage years, preferences tend to align strictly with what is popular among peer groups. As young people transition into adulthood, their willingness to explore diverse musical styles typically rebounds.

Researchers wanted to know if a person’s specific history with classical music could predict their current musical tastes. Valnea Žauhar, a…
items.t: Past experiences with classical music predict a taste for sophisticated genres

items.title: The genetic influences on drinking may shift between adolescence and early adulthood
items.summary:
An analysis of data from the Colorado Longitudinal Twin Study suggests that genetic influences on alcohol consumption change between adolescence and early adulthood. At age 17, drinking was linked to genetic predispositions for sensation seeking, while at age 23, it was linked to genetic predispositions for alcohol consumption itself. The paper was published in Drug and Alcohol Dependence .

Alcohol consumption is common during adolescence in spite of the fact that it can have negative consequences for brain development, cognitive functioning, and long-term health. Researchers have therefore sought to identify psychological and genetic factors that influence alcohol use during adolescence and early adulthood.

One important factor related to alcohol use is impulsivity, the tendency to act without thinking and to have difficulty resisting temptations. Impulsivity includes several characteristics, such as acting rashly when experiencing strong positive or negative emotions and failing to consider the consequences of one’s actions. A related but distinct characteristic is sensation seeking, the tendency to seek out exciting and stimulating experiences.

Research has consistently found that both impulsivity and sensation seeking are associated with greater alcohol consumption, although these characteristics follow different developmental patterns. Genetic studies have shown that numerous genetic variants contribute to individual differences in impulsivity, sensation seeking, and alcohol consumption. Previous findings suggest that genetic predispositions related to risk-taking…
items.t: The genetic influences on drinking may shift between adolescence and early adulthood

items.title: Brain damage linked to “pseudopsychopathy” may not reduce the will to empathize
items.summary:
People with localized damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, a lower-front brain area linked to social behavior and emotion, opted into empathy-inducing tasks in a laboratory setting just as often as healthy adults and patients with injuries elsewhere in the brain. Published in Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience , the study suggests that injury to this region does not necessarily diminish a person’s willingness to step into another’s shoes. Instead, everyday empathy struggles after such injuries may stem from trouble reading emotions rather than avoiding empathy.

The ventromedial prefrontal cortex is a region of brain tissue at the bottom middle of the frontal lobes, sitting behind the forehead and above the eye sockets. Injury here from trauma, stroke, or tumor removal can trigger dramatic shifts in personality and social judgment while sparing intelligence, memory, and speech. Since the nineteenth-century case of railroad worker Phineas Gage, who survived an iron rod passing through his skull, clinicians have observed that damage here often leaves people indifferent to social norms and others’ feelings.

Modern cases, such as a man known in medical literature by the initials EVR whose personality shifted dramatically after surgery to remove a frontal brain tumor, showed similar social detachment that clinicians have compared to psychopathic traits.

Empathy involves identifying, sharing, and understanding another person’s emotional experiences. Patients with localized areas of tissue damage, known as lesions, in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex often…
items.t: Brain damage linked to “pseudopsychopathy” may not reduce the will to empathize

items.title: New research finds high testosterone does not impair men’s emotional reframing
items.summary:
Men who routinely reframe upsetting situations in daily life tend to manage mild negative emotions more effectively when they have higher natural resting levels of the stress hormone cortisol, according to a study published in Psychoneuroendocrinology . Resting testosterone levels, examined either alone or alongside cortisol, showed no reliable link to emotional control. The results suggest that everyday psychological habits and baseline stress hormones jointly relate to how men handle mild distress.

Emotion regulation encompasses the mental processes people use to alter the intensity, duration, or expression of their feelings. One widely studied conscious strategy is cognitive reappraisal, which involves deliberately reinterpreting an upsetting scene in a less threatening or more hopeful light to soften its emotional impact. Effective use of cognitive reappraisal is associated with better psychological well-being, whereas trouble regulating emotions is common across many psychiatric disorders.

Executing this mental shift relies on communication between the prefrontal cortex, a brain region behind the forehead involved in planning and self-control, and the amygdala, an almond-shaped structure deeper in the brain that drives rapid reactions to threats. During reappraisal, the prefrontal cortex quiets activity in the amygdala. Both structures contain receptors for cortisol, the primary stress-adaptation hormone produced by the adrenal glands, and testosterone, a reproductive hormone produced mainly by the gonads that also influences social behavior.

Prior work indicated…
items.t: New research finds high testosterone does not impair men’s emotional reframing

items.title: Moderate students self-censor the most on campus, survey finds
items.summary:
Public debates over campus speech often ask whether conservative students feel pressured to hide their beliefs, yet a survey at a selective private university indicates that students with moderate opinions actually hold back the most. Right-leaning students frequently stay quiet on campus out of concern about social exclusion. Centrists, however, tend to speak up even less because they feel less certain of their positions or see contentious topics as less urgent. Distributed by the National Bureau of Economic Research in the NBER Working Paper Series , the study suggests that these silences make campus discussions sound more polarized and further left than students privately are.

Self-censorship occurs when people deliberately withhold or soften their private opinions around others, even without formal rules or official penalties barring speech. Questions about campus silence have intensified amid declining public trust in higher education and rising political polarization. Because faculty and student bodies at many selective colleges lean heavily left, critics question whether open debate is giving way to conformity, though students from underrepresented minority groups have also reported staying silent in class out of fear of backlash.

In daily campus life, students hear what classmates say out loud, not what they think privately. When people hold back unpopular views to protect their reputation or avoid friction with a vocal majority, public discussion distorts group opinion and makes the prevailing stance look closer to a consensus than it is. Competing group…
items.t: Moderate students self-censor the most on campus, survey finds

items.title: Brain surface area and cognitive ability may influence each other, genetic study suggests
items.summary:
An analysis of UK Biobank data found that people with a larger cortical surface area, the total area of the brain’s folded outer layer, tended to score slightly higher on a short test of verbal and numerical reasoning. The associations were strongest for the dorsolateral prefrontal and superior temporal regions, and genetic analyses suggested the relationship between surface area and cognitive ability may run in both directions. The paper was published in Human Brain Mapping .

Intelligence, also known as general cognitive ability or the g-factor, is strongly influenced by genetics, with genetic factors explaining up to 80% of individual differences in intelligence. However, scientists still do not fully understand how differences in brain structure relate to differences in intelligence.

Research using magnetic resonance imaging has shown that people with larger brains tend to have higher intelligence. However, the strength of this association is relatively modest. More recently, researchers have shifted their attention from overall brain volume to two characteristics of the cerebral cortex: its surface area and thickness. The cerebral cortex is the outer layer of the brain, involved in complex cognitive processes such as reasoning, memory, and decision-making.

Studies suggest that the relationship between brain volume and intelligence is largely explained by genetic factors and is primarily associated with greater cortical surface area rather than cortical thickness. Some studies have also found that higher intelligence is associated with a thinner cortex in certain…
items.t: Brain surface area and cognitive ability may influence each other, genetic study suggests

items.title: Most Teens Care, So Why Don’t They Always Help?
items.summary:
A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone. Another sees a peer being excluded from a group chat. Someone knows a friend has been struggling but hesitates before reaching out. Why?

Most adults assume the challenge is getting young people to care. But after spending years studying adolescent compassion, I have come to believe that caring may not be the central problem.

Many adolescents care deeply.

The question is what happens next.

We often imagine compassion as a straightforward process: Notice suffering, feel concern, take action. Yet anyone who has worked with adolescents knows that the path is rarely so simple. Young people are navigating friendships, social hierarchies, identity development, and concerns about belonging, all while learning how to manage their own emotions. In these moments, compassion is not simply a feeling. It is a decision unfolding within a complex social world.

In our recent research developing the Youth Compassion Measure , an assessment of compassionate responding, we find that most adolescents recognize when a peer is struggling. What varies is whether that recognition translates into helping. Across hundreds of students, four factors consistently shape whether compassion becomes action: peer dynamics, social risk, emotional regulation, and intrinsic motivation.

Understanding these factors may help parents, educators, and youth-serving professionals better support compassionate action in young people.

items.t: Most Teens Care, So Why Don’t They Always Help?

items.title: The Surprising Connection Between Grief and Gratitude
items.summary:
Life as I knew it quietly began to unravel on a drizzly January morning in 2022. 

I was standing at the kitchen sink in a puffer jacket, staring out at my favorite persimmon tree, now bare. Only weeks before, the tree had been so full of persimmons that we collected them in huge plastic garbage cans for our neighbors to take by the grocery bagful. Our Labrador-ish mutt, Buster, was fat from persimmon overconsumption. 

Back then, the kitchen was loud, warm, and colorful. Our four kids were home for the holidays, bringing hungry friends and favorite songs, their late-night cookie-baking leaving sugar dust and dirty dishes everywhere.

Now that the kids were gone, my husband Mark and I conserved energy by leaving the downstairs heat off, telling each other we couldn’t justify heating the whole house just to keep the kitchen warm. We were real empty-nesters, ready to downsize.

Within weeks, we stripped our house of everything personal. We took down family photos, scraped butterfly stickers from hidden corners, and painted over the teal walls preteen girls had decorated. All traces of our family life vanished. We put our home on the market. It was the end of an era.

In December, my seemingly super-fit mom was diagnosed with ovarian cancer. Our house still hadn’t sold—by the time we put it on the market, mortgage rates had started climbing for the first time in two decades—but I moved into my childhood bedroom at my parents’ home to help my dad care for my mom. She passed away four months later.

A week before my mom’s memorial, I myself was diagnosed with invasive breast…
items.t: The Surprising Connection Between Grief and Gratitude

items.title: At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now | Polly Hudson
items.summary:
As teenagers, my friends and I thought it was glamorous to have relationships with older men. But after the revelations about Russell Brand and David Walliams, I have started to see that period of my life in a new light

It has been a strange time to be a “woman of a certain age”, as Gregg Wallace so charmingly labelled us. Many of us were consumed by every detail of the Russell Brand trial and the David Walliams exposé. We were pleasantly surprised, albeit dazed – stunned even – by there being consequences for their behaviour, because that’s not how it usually goes, in our experience.

A few days ago, while spending time with a group of fellow certain-agers, among whom this was the main topic of discussion, as it has been pretty much everywhere I’ve been, I confessed to something of which I’m ashamed. If I had been the woman Brand was found guilty of raping – in an attack that was difficult even to read about – I worry that I would have felt powerless to complain about what had happened. I would have thought consent would be taken as a blanket statement that covered whatever followed, however horrifying and unwanted; that I’d made my bed, so was obliged to lie in it, come what may.…
items.t: At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now | Polly Hudson
